body.statement: Construct \(T_n^{\mathrm{grid}}\) over a grid of at most \(C\log n\) regularization--rank pairs with uniform asymptotic level \(\alpha\). Prove an oracle inequality attaining every radius certified by \(\mathrm{oeq{:}spectral\mbox{-}iff}\) up to an explicit logarithmic or iterated-logarithmic factor, and prove by a multi-scale mixture that no jointly adaptive test can remove that factor over the declared compact index ranges.
body.justification: The practical statistic must choose both how much to whiten and how much higher-order correction to apply without invalidating size.
body.gap: Direct MMDAgg and spectral aggregation use exchangeable raw samples; Jain and Luedtke leave data-driven Wald regularization open and calibrate only a fixed operator.
body.consumer: This replaces the heuristic Wald regularizer in the 401(k) analysis by a size-valid, data-adaptive choice.

obligation.what_is_open: The requested adaptive oracle inequality and the matching multiscale impossibility factor.
obligation.obstruction: Neither component-level critical values and power envelopes nor the spectral radii to be aggregated have been established. A shared multiplier draw alone does not imply conditional validity, and no specified family of legal multiscale alternatives is available for the lower bound.
obligation.attempted: Deterministic weighted error allocation over a logarithmic grid gives a generic uniform-size union test, but its power and unavoidable adaptation cost cannot be quantified from the frozen primitives.
obligation.partial_result:
If component tests \(\varphi_g\), indexed by a finite grid, satisfy
\(\sup_{P\in\mathcal M_0}E_P\varphi_g\le\alpha w_g\) for deterministic \(w_g>0\) with \(\sum_gw_g\le1\), then the union test satisfies
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal M_0}
P_P\{\text{at least one component rejects}\}
\le\sum_g\alpha w_g\le\alpha.
\]
This union bound is a generic size statement. The frozen core provides neither valid component critical values nor power envelopes, so it does not imply the requested oracle inequality or adaptation lower bound.
